posts.author: DJ Mathson
posts.content_md:
I think most 405 nm diodes are multimode, but I may be wrong. It would be interesting to apply the same technique to this diode as to the red ones, ie low output and rigorous temperature and current control.

Wouldn´t there be problems with fluorescence from many materials at 405 nm? I´ve experienced problems with fluorescens at 442 nm. But I suppose it would work by carefully choosing non-fluorescent colors. In DCG it would be possible to get very short exposure times at this frequency.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
OH MY GOODNESS, in DCG using the color triangle and 405, 457 and 514, we could process, red shift to get

shift 70nm to the red and get 475, 527 and 584 (blue, green and orange)

shift 86nm to the red and get 491, 543 and 600 (bluish/green, green and orangish/red) 

I was only able to use 457 and 514 because 457 and 488 were to close to see a separation with the shift of 514 to orange.

posts.author: Sergio
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** I can bearly see 405nm so one wuld need to red shift it. They are going to be cheap soon so we will get to try them.

Mine 405nm LED is also barely visible, but onto an ordinary alkaline paper that fluoresces at this WL it turns white, so you could work well with this WL in principle, also photoresists ans photopolymers are high sensitive at this WL.
